verses.text: These were the sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn. He really was the firstborn, but because he slept with one of his father's wives, his rights as the firstborn son were given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel. So Reuben is not listed in the family records as the firstborn.
Judah became the strongest of his brothers, and a ruler came from him. But the rights of the firstborn belonged to Joseph.
The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Joel's descendants were his son Shemaiah, Shemaiah's son Gog, Gog's son Shimei,
Shimei's son Micah, Micah's son Reaiah, Reaiah's son Baal,
and Baal's son Beerah. Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria took Beerah away as a prisoner. Beerah was a leader of the tribe of Reuben.
His relatives by clans, as listed in their family records, were Jeiel the chief, Zechariah,
and Bela son of Azaz, the son of Shema, the son of Joel. They lived in the area from Aroer to Nebo and Baal Meon.
To the east they settled land as far as the edge of the desert that stretches to the Euphrates River, because their herds had grown too large for the land of Gilead.
While Saul was king, they went to war against the Hagrites and defeated them. Then they lived in the Hagrites' tents throughout the whole area east of Gilead.
The tribe of Gad lived next to them, in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah.
Joel was the chief, Shapham was second, then Janai and Shaphat in Bashan.
Their relatives, by families, were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber, seven in all.
These were the sons of Abihail son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz.
Ahi son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, was the head of their families.
They lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon, as far as they reached.
All of these were recorded in the family records during the time of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel.

The tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh had forty-four thousand seven hundred and sixty men ready for war. They were brave men who could carry shields and swords, shoot with bows, and were trained for battle.
They went to war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.

God helped them in the fighting, and he handed the Hagrites and all their allies over to them. This was because they cried out to God during the battle, and he answered them because they trusted in him.
They captured the Hagrites' animals: fifty thousand camels, two hundred and fifty thousand sheep, and two thousand donkeys. They also took one hundred thousand people captive.
Many enemies were killed, because the battle was God's. And they lived in that land until they were taken away as prisoners.
The people of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They grew in number and spread from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.
These were the heads of their families: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel. They were brave warriors, famous men, and heads of their families.
But they were unfaithful to the God of their ancestors. They chased after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed ahead of them.

So the God of Israel stirred up Pul king of Assyria, also called Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria. He took the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh away as prisoners. He took them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan, where they still are today.
